title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configuration sequences and maintenance workflows for network operations (NetOps). Operational deployment requires evidence that such model outputs will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on the surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than on the model alone [1],[3]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated across NetOps and adjacent domains (DevOps, program repair), but paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited [2],[7].

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid), diagnostics explaining ceiling effects, and concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up confirmatory designs that would permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLMs for NetOps and AIOps span intent‑based configuration, runbook generation, root cause analysis (RCA), and nascent self‑healing architectures. Empirical reports and surveys document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines and knowledge anchoring [1],[5]. Generate–validate–repair patterns appear across software repair and DevOps literature as practical defenses against hallucinated outputs [2],[6]. Batfish and related static/emulation tools are recognized building blocks for deterministic validation of network configurations; lessons from Batfish development illustrate the practical value and limits of rule‑based verification in network‑change workflows [7].

Two methodological gaps motivated our paired design. First, many prior comparisons use nonpaired samples or permit different generation semantics per arm, complicating attribution of safety gains to validators versus different model draws. Second, existing benchmarks often emphasize QA/relevance metrics or log/RCA tasks but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators and paired protocols that preserve or control the initial candidate sampling variance [6]. Our preregistered shared_initial_candidate experiment directly isolates validator/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates, closing a targeted methodological gap in the literature.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1. The preregistration fixed: the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate); model and adapter (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1); deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy; repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents); and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). All parameters were frozen prior to observing outputs and are archived in the execution manifest (execution/model_configuration.json and preregistration manifest).

Generation semantics clarification (required by peer review). Generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both the baseline and guarded arms per paired intent; therefore the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on that same first‑pass candidate and does not measure any effect of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance. This sentence restates the preregistered choice and explains the statistical meaning of a degenerate contingency.

Modeling and orchestration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and provider = "openai_responses"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing sequence, precondition, protected‑interface and reachability checks. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Fixed provider parameters archived in execution/model_configuration.json (max_output_tokens=2000; maximum_attempts_per_call=1; reasoning_effort="minimal").

Task bank and sampling. The preregistration specified deterministic task selection (task_count = 200 pairs; planned_episode_count = 400) using the adapter's index rule. Task payloads encode initial_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, workflow_policies (final_group_constraints and minimum_active_in_groups), and difficulty metadata. The archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑task metadata; manifest entries include difficulty.level tags such as "very_hard" and "extreme" (manifest available in the evidence bundle). Selection is fixed and outcome‑independent by design.

Interventions and scoring. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate without gating. Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the preregistered deterministic gate applied an accept/reject policy and allowed up to one automated repair attempt when violations occurred. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported after candidate stabilization (scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation). Per‑episode validator traces (validation_before/validation_after), repair flags, and scoring_reason_code are archived under execution/scoring/*. Representative scoring records are included in the evidence bundle.

Confirmatory analysis (frozen). The primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 on complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 200). The registered test is an exact two‑sided McNemar–equivalent on the paired binary unsafe_flag, with the paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and limited retry rules were preregistered; the run produced no retriable infrastructure failures. All analysis outputs and logs are archived (analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed as preregistered: started_at_utc = 2026‑08‑31T13:49:34.191203+00:00 and completed_at_utc = 2026‑08‑31T14:14:32.660268+00:00 (execution manifest). Planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair); hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200. Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode_accounting_consistent = true and all audits passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. The exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] using bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The degenerate CI is an arithmetic consequence of zero discordant pairs under the registered estimand.

Repair and validator diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; repair_provider_trace_path fields are null in scoring artifacts. Validator traces per episode record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and final_state snapshots. Representative episodes (task‑000004 through task‑000008) in execution/scoring/* show violation_count = 0 and empty violations arrays for all completed episodes; scoring_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION in every scoring record. These per‑episode artifacts substantiate that the validator recognized and accepted the generated sequences without invoking repair.

Latency notes. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics required a single model call per pair, model_call accounting equals 200. The guarded pipeline incurred deterministic validator execution time but no repair cycles; timing logs in execution/execution_log.jsonl and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl show median additional per‑pair wall time was dominated by deterministic validator evaluation rather than repair attempts. Exact latency distributions and medians are archived and reproducible from execution/execution_log.jsonl.

Missingness and contamination. missingness_summary shows complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. contamination_summary.csv is empty (no flagged contamination). Deterministic reconciliation confirms all deterministic consistency checks passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the chosen synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; therefore the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The archived artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/scoring/*.json) support this interpretation.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. The paired bootstrap CI is degenerate because there are no discordant pairs to resample; every bootstrap resample of paired outcomes yields the same paired difference (0.0), producing zero empirical variance and thus CI = [0.0,0.0]. The analysis executor parameters and seed (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000) are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl), and the zero variance is a legitimate inferential outcome rather than an analysis error.

Ceiling‑effect contributors (artifact‑supported). The manifest and representative task traces point to three contributors: (1) task‑generation alignment—deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced intents whose required sequences closely match the prompt schema and the model's expected canonical output form (task_manifest entries include required_sequence and expected_final_state fields that mirror normalized_response content); (2) validator tightness—the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ruleset encoded sequencing and precondition checks consistent with the generator's constraints, raising the probability that syntactically correct candidates pass; and (3) the shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model variance that might have produced repairs or discordant outcomes. Representative artifact paths that document these points include execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*.txt, and execution/scoring/*.json.

Design recommendations supported by artifacts. To permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate effects we recommend: (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution seeds to raise baseline unsafe rates (the archived manifest encodes generator seeds and difficulty labels that can be extended); (b) changing generation semantics to independent per‑condition sampling or multiple independent samples per condition, which requires increased model_call budgets and yields an estimand capturing guarded‑conditioned regeneration and sampling variance; (c) increasing automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness when initial violations are present; and (d) evaluating multiple model variants, temperatures, or decoding settings to reveal model variance effects. Execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl provide the knobs and provenance required to implement these follow‑ups reproducibly.

Reproducibility pathways. All per‑episode responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/results.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Researchers can replay the exact run under the same adapter to reproduce the confirmatory null result; they can modify manifest seeds to insert adversarial cases or alter generation semantics to independent sampling and rerun, with model_call accounting and logs captured in execution/execution_log.jsonl. Detailed artifact locations and representative SHA‑256s are included in the execution_manifest and model_configuration artifacts.

Threats to validity (summary). Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally limit inference to validator/gate effects and exclude guarded‑conditioned regeneration effects. Construct validity: the unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage of sequencing and precondition rules and therefore does not capture all possible operational hazards (e.g., transient performance issues, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules). External validity: single model, single validator, synthetic tasks, and sandboxed validation limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: the run was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point paired reductions per the preregistration power plan, but the observed degenerate concordance precludes observing reductions under this sample because baseline unsafe occurrences were absent. Each threat is documented and traceable to archived artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model, the synthetic task bank, the deterministic selection, the validator ruleset, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., independent condition generation, adversarial inputs, multiple model samples). We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions. All core artifacts and analysis outputs supporting these conclusions are archived and referenced in this manuscript's evidence bundle.

Models and tools: single LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); orchestration/adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Human role and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the topical family and constrained the initial prompt pre‑lock; all literature review, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer‑review emulation, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the lock. Generation semantics clarification: the executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled generation reused by both arms per pair); therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates rather than effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. The preregistration id is autocand_A1_prereg_v1.
limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
